title: Creative Diversification: Why 50 Ad Assets May Be Only 2 Concepts & How to Fix
summary: How to audit creative diversity and turn the findings into your next production brief.
body_markdown:
A paid social production report can show fifty new ad assets while the next campaign tests **only two ideas** .


**Creative diversification** means expanding the range of ideas and formats in your ads. To assess it, you need to distinguish a new persuasive idea from another execution or delivery version of an existing one.


Different placements need different dimensions. Localization can add more files. Each version may require production work, but the total does not tell you how many distinct reasons to consider your product the campaign will test.


Before requesting another batch, audit which concepts the account already tests and what each proposed variation is meant to teach you.


## A GetCrux field note: Creative volume can hide a narrow concept pool


This article grew out of our conversations with advertising teams about what they need when they ask for "more creative."


- **Travel and accommodation:** A marketplace described polished ads that looked similar, with too little variety for refreshes.
- **Quick-commerce delivery:** A team wanted to explore visual styles beyond its usual video output.
- **Ride-hailing and delivery:** A platform discussion examined whether hundreds of variations of a winning ad justified the production work.


These conversations pointed to a distinction that production reports can obscure. More files can help a team cover placements and markets. More executions can help it improve an existing idea. Testing another reason to choose the product requires **a different concept** .


That distinction changes the next brief. Before setting an asset target, ask:


> Which ideas are we adding to the account, and what will each execution help us learn?


Our takeaway is to record concepts separately from executions and delivery versions, with format tracked alongside them. This gives the team a clearer account of what the next batch will test.


The fifty-file example below is hypothetical. It illustrates this counting problem.

## What counts as a different ad concept?


- **Concept:** The central persuasive idea an ad tests—the reason to consider the product.
- **Execution:** A particular expression of that idea, such as a different opening, visual treatment, or way of presenting evidence.
- **Export:** A file prepared for delivery, such as a placement adaptation or another language version of the same idea.


A different crop usually preserves the original concept. A rewritten headline may also preserve it. A new hook can introduce a useful test, but the team should be able to explain what changed and what it expects to learn.


For example, an ad that promises to save money on groceries might open with a receipt, a price comparison, or a customer describing their weekly bill. Those executions can test different ways of presenting the same price argument.


An ad about getting a forgotten ingredient before dinner makes a different argument. It addresses a specific situation where the customer needs the service.


Format is a separate dimension of creative diversity.


A product demonstration and an infographic can communicate the same promise through different formats. Testing both may help the team understand how to explain that promise. The concept count can remain unchanged while the campaign explores another way of communicating it.


Record both dimensions so the next brief makes clear whether the team wants different ideas, different formats, or further executions of an existing concept.


## How fifty ad assets can contain two concepts


Consider a grocery delivery campaign with two concepts.


One makes a price argument: save money on the weekly shop.


The second addresses a specific situation: get a forgotten ingredient when dinner plans change.


The team produces five executions of each concept. It then creates five delivery versions of every execution.


The production report now contains:


- **Two concepts.**
- **Ten executions.**
- **Fifty exports.**


Fifty files is an accurate production count. The campaign still has two central ideas to test.


This distinction helps clarify a request for "more creative." The team might need more delivery versions for additional placements. It might need a better execution of the price argument. Or it might need to explore a customer situation neither concept addresses.


Each request leads to different production work.


## How to audit creative diversity in a paid social account


The audit should help the team decide what to produce next. Start with the actual ads and connect each execution to a question the team wants to answer.


### 1. Group ads by their central idea


Review the assets together. Give each concept group a sentence that describes the argument it makes.


"Convenience" is often too broad to guide production. "Avoid another grocery trip when you discover a missing ingredient" gives the team a specific situation to work with.


If two ads belong in the same group, explain why. If the team disagrees, resolve the definition before treating the concept count as precise.


Naming conventions can help organize the review, but review the assets themselves. A filename may omit the use case or argument visible in the ad.


### 2. Write down what each execution tests


For every execution, complete this sentence:


> **This version changes ___ because we want to learn ___** .


A shorter opening might test whether viewers understand the use case sooner. A different proof point might test which evidence makes the promise more credible.


"Make another version" leaves the learning objective unclear.


Some files exist to meet delivery requirements. Record that purpose directly. A placement adaptation can justify production work without being a new experiment.


### 3. Check which customer needs and formats receive attention


Look across the concept groups.


Which customer situations appear repeatedly? Which product benefits receive little attention? Are most executions using the same visual treatment?


The answer should identify a gap the next brief can address.


A concept may need another execution because the existing ads explain it poorly. A campaign may need a different format to demonstrate the product. A narrow set of messages may need fresh customer research before production begins.


Brand constraints belong in this review too. A team working within approved templates can still explore different customer situations or arguments.


### 4. Check delivery before judging a concept


An account may contain several concepts while most spend goes to one of them. That limits what the team can conclude about the others.


Record how much exposure each concept received alongside the relevant performance results. Low spend can leave an idea insufficiently evaluated.


**Spend alone does not establish business impact** . Assessing that requires the outcome data and measurement method appropriate to the campaign.


Use the audit to distinguish a concept the team has evaluated from one that is present in the account but still has an unanswered question.


### 5. Assign a purpose to the next batch


Use the audit to decide what each proposed execution should accomplish.


An execution might refine an established concept, test an unaddressed customer situation, or explore another format. The brief should state its purpose and how the team will evaluate the result.


The mix depends on what the account has already tested, what remains uncertain, and the production capacity available.


## Turn the audit into the next creative brief


Before commissioning more versions of a winning ad, identify what remains unresolved.


Perhaps the opening needs improvement. Perhaps another proof point could make the promise more credible. Perhaps a different format could explain the product more clearly.


If the team cannot identify a useful question, the brief may need fresh research. Customer objections and examples outside the category can suggest ideas the current account has not tested.


Return to the hypothetical grocery delivery campaign. Its existing concepts address price savings and forgotten ingredients.


A brief for the next batch could specify:


- **Refine the price concept** by testing an itemized basket comparison against the existing savings claim.
- **Test a product demonstration** for the forgotten-ingredient concept.
- **Explore a new concept** about reducing the effort of planning the weekly shop, treating that customer need as a hypothesis to investigate.
- List the required placement and language versions separately.


The first two tasks develop existing concepts. The third explores another reason to consider the service. The delivery requirements determine how many files production needs to prepare.


That brief gives the team something more specific than "produce fifty assets."


Before approving the batch, check that each proposed execution has a stated purpose and that **delivery versions are counted separately** . The production total will then show the workload, while the concept list shows which ideas the campaign is intended to test.
